challenge.q: Why do all living things need food?
challenge.answer: Food is their source of energy for life processes.
mixups: Food keeps them from feeling bored.
Food is needed only by animals that move.
Food makes them heavier, and that is its only use.
challenge.why: Food is a source of energy. Living things use that energy for life processes such as moving, growing and repairing.

challenge.q: A pupil says, "Only living things that can move need food for energy." Is the pupil right?
challenge.answer: No. A mould never moves, but it still needs food for energy.
mixups: Yes. Only living things that can move need food for energy.
Yes. A mould grows without needing food.
Yes. Growing does not use energy, only moving and running do.
challenge.why: The mould covered more area when it was given more food. Every living thing needs food for energy, whether it moves or not.

challenge.q: Why was each amount of food tested more than once?
challenge.answer: Repeating and averaging makes the result more reliable.
mixups: To use up all the food in the bowl before the next test.
To tire the animal out.
So that each run gives a different conclusion.
challenge.why: One reading can be a little high or a little low. Repeating and taking the average gives a more reliable result.

bench.name: Energy Labels Lab
bench.subtitle: Comparing the energy stored in food

aim: A shelf holds five food samples, each with a label card face down. Beside it are a portion tray and a rack of food packets. Read the energy value on each label and compare.
bigIdea: Different foods store different amounts of energy. A bigger portion of the same food stores more energy in total, but the type of food still matters. Food labels report the energy value of a food, so foods can be compared. Reading labels helps us choose a variety of foods for a balanced diet.

challenge.q: A pupil says, "A food that weighs more always has a higher energy value than a lighter food." Is the pupil right?
challenge.answer: No. The type matters: 10 g of peanut has more energy than 10 g of apple.
mixups: Yes. A heavier food always has a higher energy value than a lighter food.
Yes. The sweeter food always has the highest energy value.
Yes. A food label shows only the total mass of the food, not its energy value.
challenge.why: Different foods store different amounts of energy in each gram. Mass alone does not tell you the energy value.

challenge.q: The same snack is served as a 20 g portion and a 40 g portion. Which has more energy in total?
challenge.answer: The 40 g portion, because there is more of the same food.
mixups: The 20 g portion, because a smaller portion is packed with energy.
Both are the same, because it is the same food.
Neither. Portion size has nothing to do with energy.
challenge.why: A bigger portion of the same food has more energy in total. The value for each gram stays the same.

challenge.q: To compare two foods fairly from their labels, what must you do?
challenge.answer: Read the same column, such as "per gram", on both labels.
mixups: Read whichever number looks biggest on each of the two labels.
Compare the colours and the pictures on the two labels.
Taste both foods first.
challenge.why: A fair comparison keeps everything the same except the food. Reading the same amount, such as each gram, on every label does that.

scriptCautions: The bench gives energy values in "units" per gram, not calories. The textbook figures are 4 calories per gram for carbohydrate or protein and 9 for fat (P6 style guide section 1). Do not present the bench numbers as calories.

bench.subtitle: Where a living thing's energy comes from

aim: Find out where a living thing gets its energy: change the light on a patch of grass, measure the energy at each link of a food chain, then trace three animals back to their first source of energy.
bigIdea: The Sun is the primary source of energy for almost all living things. Plants trap light energy and store it in the food they make. That energy passes along a food chain, but only part of it passes on at each link.
safety: A real sun lamp gets hot. Never touch the bulb, and never look straight into a bright lamp.

badge.line: You measured the energy at every link and traced three animals back to the Sun.

challenge.q: A pupil says, "Animals get their energy from the food they eat, not from the Sun." What is missing from this idea?
challenge.answer: That energy can be traced back to the Sun, so animals depend on it too.
mixups: Nothing. Animals get all their energy from food, so the Sun does not matter.
Animals that eat other animals do not depend on the Sun at all.
Animals get their energy from the soil and the water instead.
challenge.why: An animal gets energy from its food, but that energy first came from the Sun, trapped by a plant. Every trace leads back to the Sun.

challenge.q: In the chain grass → grasshopper → frog, which has the least energy available?
challenge.answer: The frog, because only part of the energy passes on.
mixups: The grass, because it gives all its energy away.
They all have the same, because energy only moves along.
The frog has the most, because it is the biggest.
challenge.why: About 10 units at the grass became about 3 at the grasshopper and about 1 at the frog. Only part passes on at each link.

challenge.q: A shark never leaves the sea and never touches a plant. Does its energy still trace back to the Sun?
challenge.answer: Yes. Its food chain starts with living things that trap light energy.
mixups: No. The shark makes its own energy, so it does not need the Sun.
No. The shark gets its energy from the sea water itself, not from food.
No. Only land animals depend on the Sun, because plants grow on land.
challenge.why: The shark eats fish, which eat smaller living things, back to those that trap light energy from the Sun. Every chain starts there.

bench.name: Energy Chain Lab
bench.subtitle: Telling an energy transfer story correctly

aim: A story board holds picture cards of a producer and several consumers. A second board shows how food chains join into a food web. Tell each energy story the right way round.
bigIdea: The arrow in a food chain points from the eaten to the eater, showing the direction in which energy passes. A food web is made of several food chains joined together. Energy passes along a chain, but only part of it passes at each link. The living thing furthest from the producer has the least energy available.

challenge.q: A pupil writes: snake → frog → grasshopper → grass. What is wrong?
challenge.answer: The arrows are the wrong way round. It should start: grass → grasshopper.
mixups: Nothing. The arrow points from the animal to the food it has just eaten.
The arrows should point to the biggest animal.
The direction of the arrows does not matter.
challenge.why: An arrow points from the eaten to the eater, showing the direction in which energy passes. The chain must start with the producer.

challenge.q: A chain has 10.0 units of energy at the grass, 2.8 at the grasshopper and 0.8 at the frog. Why does the frog have so little?
challenge.answer: Only part passes on at each link. The rest is given out as heat.
mixups: The frog is small, so it cannot hold much energy.
The frog did not eat enough grasshoppers to fill up.
The energy should be the same at every link, so the readings are wrong.
challenge.why: Each living thing uses energy for its life processes and gives energy out as heat. Only what is left can pass to the next link.

challenge.q: Why does every food chain start with a producer?
challenge.answer: A producer makes its own food, using light energy.
mixups: A producer is the smallest living thing.
A producer has less energy than the consumers that eat it.
A producer eats the consumers.
challenge.why: Plants are producers. They trap light energy and store it in the food they make, and that energy then passes along the chain.

written.model: A food web is several food chains joined together. It shows how the living things in a place feed on one another.

it shows all the feeding connections between the living things in a place
doNotAccept: one very long food chain
a list of the animals in a habitat
a web that a spider makes to catch food
a food chain (no mention of several chains joined)

written.q: On the story board, the correct link was grass → grasshopper, not grasshopper → grass. Explain why the arrow points this way. [2]
written.model: The arrow shows the direction in which energy passes. The grasshopper eats the grass, so energy passes from the grass to the grasshopper, and the arrow points from the grass to the grasshopper.
doNotAccept: the arrow means 'eats', so the grass eats the grasshopper
the arrow points to the bigger or stronger living thing
the grass comes first because it is a plant (no mention of energy)
the arrow shows which way the animal moves

written.model: Most living things eat more than one kind of food and are eaten by more than one kind of animal. So the same living thing, like the snake, is part of more than one food chain, and the chains join at it to make a food web.
doNotAccept: the chains join to make one longer chain
all animals eat grass
the animals live in the same place (no mention of feeding)

parts.label: Part (a): Artificial light and hatchlings reaching the sea
parts.title: Artificial light and hatchlings reaching the sea
parts.does: Three trials per light setting average automatically; the run button stays grey until the three chips are set correctly.
parts.predictQ: With artificial light present, will fewer or more hatchlings crawl to the sea successfully?
parts.takeaway: Artificial light near a nesting beach is a negative human impact. It can lower the number of hatchlings that reach the sea safely.

predictOptions.reason: Artificial light confuses hatchlings, who naturally head toward the brighter horizon over the sea.
Light helps hatchlings see the way to the sea better.
Hatchlings always find the sea using smell, not light.

parts.observeQ: What was the average number of hatchlings reaching the sea with artificial light present?

variables.changed: artificial light (off · on)
variables.measured: number of hatchlings, out of 20, reaching the sea in a fixed time
variables.kept: number of hatchlings released, 20 · distance to the sea · time given

parts.graph: average number reaching the sea against light setting, the pupil taps the bar order that fits.

parts.label: Part (b): Litter and hatchlings reaching the sea in time
parts.title: Litter and hatchlings reaching the sea in time
parts.does: Three trials per litter amount average automatically.
parts.predictQ: As more litter is placed on the beach path, what will happen to the number of hatchlings reaching the sea in time?
parts.takeaway: Litter left on a beach is a negative human impact. It can block or slow the path hatchlings take to reach the sea.

predictOptions.reason: Litter blocks and slows down the hatchlings' path to the sea.
Hatchlings can always crawl around any amount of litter.
Litter gives hatchlings something to hide behind from predators, so more survive.

parts.observeQ: What was the average number reaching the sea in time with a lot of litter?

variables.changed: amount of litter (none · some · a lot)
variables.measured: number of hatchlings, out of 20, reaching the sea in a fixed time
variables.kept: distance to the sea · number of hatchlings, 20 · time limit · no artificial light

parts.graph: average number reaching the sea against litter amount, the pupil taps the bar order that fits.

parts.label: Part (c): Combined conservation action
parts.title: Combined conservation action
parts.does: A what-if slider lets the pupil adjust light shielding and litter clearing separately and see the predicted number reaching the sea update live before running the real trial; three trials per level then average.
parts.predictQ: Which level of conservation action will let the most hatchlings reach the sea?
parts.predictAnswer: Full, litter cleared and light shielded
parts.takeaway: Taking more than one conservation action together, such as clearing litter and reducing artificial light, works best. It increases an animal's chances of survival more than taking just one action.

predictOptions.reason: Conservation actions don't really change survival chances.
Clearing litter alone fixes the whole problem.

predictOptions.text: Full, litter cleared and light shielded
predictOptions.reason: Clearing litter and shielding the light together remove both negative impacts.
